studies.title: Preferring Others While Short
studies.meaning: The people described are named by where they were rather than by what they did: they had settled the home and the faith before the arrivals came. Three things follow. They love the newcomers, they feel no want in their chests for what the newcomers were given, and they prefer others over themselves while short themselves. The closing clause moves the difficulty inward: what has to be escaped is not poverty but the grasping of one's own soul.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, after the expulsion of a Medinan tribe and the distribution of what was left behind. The ayat just before assign that property largely to the emigrants from Mecca, who had arrived with nothing, rather than to the people of Medina who had hosted them for years. This ayah describes how the hosts received that decision, and the classical sources treat it as praise of a specific group at a specific moment.

keyTerms.note: A verb for taking a place as a dwelling. It governs two objects here, the home and the faith, so the grammar puts belief and residence in the same category: something you move into and live in.
From a root meaning to choose and to leave a trace. The word became the classical name for giving away what you need yourself, and it is distinguished from generosity with a surplus.
A stronger word than ordinary meanness, combining the desire to keep with the desire to acquire. Attaching it to the soul makes it a condition to be rescued from rather than a habit to be corrected.
The word names a chink or opening, the gaps in a wall, and by extension a hole in a person's own provision. It pictures poverty as something you can see through rather than as a quantity.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: When the Meccans arrived in Medina they had no houses, no land and no trade contacts. The people of Medina paired off with them, sharing homes, splitting date palms and finding them work. The arrangement lasted for years and cost the hosts real income in a town where cultivable land was scarce and irrigation expensive. This ayah was heard by people still living inside that arrangement.
studies.didYouKnow: The closing clause of this ayah appears a second time in the Quran, word for word, in a later surah, where it follows an instruction to spend rather than a portrait of a community. The repetition detaches it from this occasion: what is described here as the achievement of one group in one year is stated elsewhere as a general condition of success.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah locates the obstacle precisely. Not wealth, not poverty, and not the other person: the thing standing between a human being and success is named as the grasping quality of his own soul, and the verb used for escaping it is passive. You are protected from it rather than defeating it. That makes generosity, in this description, less an achievement than a rescue, which is why the passage reads as praise without any trace of flattery.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the clause about being saved from one's own grasping, attaching it to spending rather than to a community.
Extends the portrait to later generations, whose share is to ask forgiveness and to carry no resentment.
Shows the same preference in a single act, food given away by people who wanted it themselves.

studies.applyIt: Give something away this week that you would actually like to keep. Not money you will not miss. A ticket, an afternoon, the last of something. Then notice the small internal argument that starts up while you do it. That argument is what the ayah names, and being able to hear it is most of the work.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: What You Sent For Tomorrow
studies.meaning: The word for tomorrow is doing a lot of work. A whole hereafter is named by the ordinary word for the next day, which shortens the distance to it and makes the accounting immediate. The instruction is to look, and what is to be looked at is what has already been sent ahead, not what is intended. Awareness of God frames the sentence on both sides, repeated before and after, which is unusual even in the Quran.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at the end of a surah about a broken alliance and an expulsion from Medina. The ayah before closes a short parable in which one party urges another into ruin and then disowns him. That is the immediate background: people who had made promises to each other and did not keep them. The instruction to examine your own account follows directly on a picture of misplaced trust.

keyTerms.note: The plain word for the following day, indefinite here, so it reads as a tomorrow rather than the tomorrow. Classical readers note the effect: the last day is spoken of as near enough to plan for.

A verb of sending something on in advance, used of provisions dispatched before a journey. It makes deeds into baggage that has already left, which is why the ayah asks you to look rather than to decide.
An imperative of seeing, applied to a soul rather than to a person, and phrased in the third person so it lands as a general instruction. The verb is inspection rather than reflection.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan sent goods ahead. A merchant with a long journey dispatched part of his load with an earlier group so it would be waiting at the other end, and the practice had its own vocabulary. What went forward was gone; you could not adjust it once it left. The ayah uses that verb for deeds, addressed to people who had sent consignments ahead and knew the feeling of watching them leave.
studies.didYouKnow: Awareness of God is commanded twice inside this single ayah, once before the instruction and once after it, a doubling the Quran uses sparingly. A few ayat later the surah ends with a run of divine names, one of the densest concentrations anywhere in the Book, so the chapter closes on the one being feared.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Self-examination is put in the imperative and given an object, which distinguishes it from anxiety. You are not told to worry about the outcome; you are told to inspect a record. The choice of the word for tomorrow also does something specific to the doctrine. By using the everyday term rather than a technical one, the passage makes the hereafter continuous with ordinary planning rather than a separate subject a person visits occasionally.

crossReferences.why: Names the opposite of this inspection, forgetting God and losing sight of oneself in the same movement.
Uses the same verb for what was sent forward and adds what was left behind, at the moment of knowing.
Promises that what is sent ahead is found again, which is the encouraging half of the same image.

studies.applyIt: Take five minutes tonight and write down what you actually did today, not what you meant to do. No verdict at the end, no resolutions. The ayah asks for a look at the record, and most people find the surprise is not in what is bad but in how much of the day is unaccounted for.
